sec.title: Background
sec.p: The Oncotype DX Breast Recurrence Score® test is prognostic for distant recurrence in hormone receptor positive (HR+), human epidermal growth factor 2 negative (HER2-) early-stage breast cancer. It is the only multigene assay able to predict chemotherapy benefit, validated by evidence from randomized controlled trials. Using a Japanese public healthcare payer perspective, a cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted comparing the Oncotype DX® test to clinico-pathological risk assessment in women with node-negative (N0), HR+/HER2- early breast cancer.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A decision-tree stratified patients according to their Recurrence Score® (RS®) result and adjuvant chemotherapy allocation. A Markov model was used to capture lifetime costs and outcomes of the chosen treatment. Distributions of clinical risk in N0 patients were derived from the TAILORx trial. Distant recurrence probability conditional on RS result was calculated using TAILORx and NSABP-20 studies. Endocrine and chemoendocrine therapy selection was informed by a Clinical Expert Survey and the literature. Drugs and medical device costs were obtained from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The Oncotype DX test was dominant (i.e. cost-saving and more effective) as it generated more quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) (0.207) at a lower cost (-¥649,596) compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment in the overall population. Cost savings were primarily driven by a lower incidence of distant recurrence (-¥1,007,177). The Oncotype DX test was dominant in all subgroups except for one, which was cost-effective.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Use of the Oncotype DX test to guide treatment decisions improves patient outcomes while reducing healthcare costs for N0 HR+/HER2- early-stage breast cancer in Japan.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In Japan, breast cancer is the most common cancer in women and the fifth most prevalent cancer overall, with an estimated 91,100 new cases diagnosed in 2024 [1]. Early-stage invasive breast cancer (defined as tumor stage I, II or IIIA) is a heterogeneous, phenotypically diverse disease composed of several molecular subtypes that have distinct responses to therapy [2]. In Japan, 69% of all breast cancer tumors are subtype hormone receptor positive (HR+) and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative (HER2-) [3]. When treated appropriately, this subtype demonstrates the highest survival rate amongst breast cancer patients [4, 5]. For the HR+/HER2- subtype, adjuvant treatment using endocrine or chemoendocrine therapy is the standard of care to preventing recurrence following surgery [6–9]. However, the patients for whom chemotherapy confers a benefit remain a matter of conjecture among clinicians [10, 11]. In Japan, historically, clinico-pathological factors (referred to as clinical risk factors in this report) have been used to guide treatment decisions in the adjuvant setting [11]. Clinical risk factors considered include nodal status, tumor size, grade, patient age and menopausal status, along with immunohistochemistry factors such as Ki67. Although clinical risk factors alone are prognostically useful, the predictive benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy remains unknown using this approach, which leads to sub-optimal outcomes through over- or under-use of chemotherapy.

The Oncotype DX Breast Recurrence Score test (the Oncotype DX test) assesses expression of 21 genes in tumor tissue and generates a Recurrence Score (RS) result, which provides both prognostic and predictive information to support adjuvant chemotherapy decision-making [12–14]. The test has been validated in multiple clinical studies including the prospective randomized TAILORx study, and to date, it is the only multigene assay with the ability to predict chemotherapy benefit [12–14]. The test has been incorporated into various international guidelines including the Japanese clinical guidelines and is currently reimbursed in Japan [6–9, 11].

A previous study, published in 2014, reported that the Oncotype DX test was cost-effective compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment in Japanese N0, HR+/HER2- early breast cancer patients [15]. This study was published prior to completion of the TAILORx clinical trial [12]. Recent published studies conducted in the US and UK, demonstrated that the Oncotype DX test is dominant (cost-saving and more effective) compared to using clinico-pathological risk assessment in N0, HR+/HER2- early breast cancer patients [16–18].

The aim of this study was to estimate the cost-effectiveness of using the Oncotype DX test to inform adjuvant chemotherapy decision-making compared to clinical risk factors alone for N0, HR+/HER2- early breast cancer, using the latest clinical trial outcomes and current clinical practice in Japan.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: A previously published model comparing the Oncotype DX test versus clinico-pathological risk assessment in early-stage HR+/HER2- breast cancer, used in UK and US analyses, was adapted to the Japanese healthcare setting, in accordance with Japanese best practice guidelines for health technology assessment [16, 17, 19]. The model, developed in Microsoft Excel® (Redmond, WA, 98052), uses a decision-tree to stratify patients by RS result and assigned adjuvant treatment. Following the decision-tree component, patients entered a Markov model with 6-month cycles, which captured the long-term outcomes of treatment. Markov health states included recurrence-free, distant recurrence, long-term treatment-related adverse events (AEs) (acute myeloid leukemia [AML] and congestive heart failure [CHF], which are associated with chemotherapy use) and death. Recurrence-free patients were assumed to be at risk of distant recurrence and long-term AEs. Transition to death was modelled from all health states. A model schematic is presented in Fig. 1. Using the current Japanese health technology assessment (HTA) guidelines, the analysis adopted a Japanese public healthcare payer perspective using the 2024 cost year, and incorporated a 2% annual discount rate applied to costs and QALYs [19]. No inflation adjustments were applied as all input costs were from 2024. A summary table of the key model inputs is presented (Table 1), with a full table of inputs provided in the supplementary materials (Table S10).

sec.p: The population consisted of Japanese women with newly diagnosed N0 HR+/HER2- early-stage invasive breast cancer. A subgroup analysis was conducted using age (≤ 50 years, > 50 years, all) and clinical risk (low and high). Clinical risk definitions were based on an exploratory analysis from the TAILORx study [12]. Low clinical risk was defined as low histologic grade and tumor size ≤ 3 cm, intermediate histologic grade and tumor size ≤ 2 cm or high histologic grade and tumor size ≤ 1 cm. All other cases were considered high clinical risk.

RS categories were aligned with those used in the TAILORx study (low: 0–10, intermediate: 11–25, high: 26–100), and previously published cost-effectiveness modelling [12, 16, 17]. On the recommendation of Japanese clinical experts consulted in their capacity as an Advisory Board funded by the sponsor in 2024 (Advisory Board, 2024), and to accommodate different chemotherapy probabilities between RS results in the range of 11–25, the intermediate RS distribution was split equally into three further categories: intermediate-low (RS: 11–15), intermediate-mid (RS: 16–20) and intermediate-high (RS: 21–25).

To inform Japanese specific clinical practice and model inputs, a Clinical Expert Survey was conducted in 2024, with data collected from clinicians (N = 8) experienced in using the Oncotype DX test in Japan in breast cancer treatment (Clinical Expert Survey, 2024). The survey was used to help determine chemotherapy allocation based on RS results when using Oncotype DX test in each subgroup (≤ 50 years and > 50 years, low and high clinical risk) defined in TAILORx. For N0 overall, chemotherapy allocation values were calculated weighted by the proportion of each subgroup from TAILORx [20].

In the comparator group of clinico-pathological risk assessment, chemotherapy allocation for each high clinical risk subgroup was informed by the clinical trial literature [21]. Due to the absence of published data for low clinical risk, the chemotherapy allocation in each low clinical risk subgroup was informed by the Clinical Expert Survey. The survey also revealed the distribution of chemotherapy regimens currently used in Japan. As in the Oncotype DX group, chemotherapy allocation values for N0 overall in the comparator group were calculated weighted by the proportion of each subgroup from TAILORx. The proportion of patients assigned to chemotherapy following Oncotype DX test and clinico-pathological risk assessment in each subgroup is shown in Fig. 2 and Table S1, while that of N0 overall is shown in Table 1.

sec.p: Distant recurrence probability for RS 0–10 (endocrine therapy), 11–25 (endocrine and chemoendocrine therapy), and 26–100 (chemoendocrine therapy) were obtained from TAILORx using 9-year distant recurrence-free interval (DRFI), adjusted to a 6-month probability to align with the cycle length [12]. No chemotherapy benefit was assumed for RS 0–10. For RS result 11–25, the benefit was calculated from distant recurrence probabilities for intermediate RS from TAILORx for chemotherapy and no chemotherapy [20]. Distant recurrence probability for RS result ≥ 26 for endocrine therapy alone was calculated using the difference between endocrine and chemoendocrine therapy in the NSABP B-20 study, reported as a proportional hazard ratio of 0.27 [22]. It was assumed that local recurrence occurred in 10.5% of distant recurrence [23]. The key clinical model inputs are presented in Table 1.

AML and CHF were modelled as long-term AEs of anthracycline and taxane-based chemotherapies only. The probability of AML was derived from a published meta-analysis [24]. CHF probability was calculated by applying a hazard for chemotherapy-related CHF (1.61) to standard age-adjusted incidence of CHF, sourced from the literature [25, 26].

Mortality risk in the recurrence-free health state was calculated using current Japanese general population values, with no excess mortality risk assumed (Supplementary Material) [27]. Distant recurrence mortality risk was calculated using the median overall survival from the Japanese subgroup analysis of the MONARCH 2 trial, converted to a 6-month mortality probability [28]. The mortality risk for AML was based on survival of patients with chemotherapy-related AML enrolled in an international study, adjusted to 6-month probability [24]. Age-dependent CHF mortality probability was obtained from the literature [29].

The cost of the Oncotype DX test used was the list price in Japan (¥435,000) [30]. Distribution of adjuvant endocrine, chemoendocrine therapy, and supportive treatment regimens (e.g., growth factors) was informed by the survey (Clinical Expert Survey, 2024). Dosage regimens were based on the Japanese clinical guidelines and combined with official tariffs to estimate the total cost of treatment for each endocrine and chemotherapy regimen (Supplementary Material) [11, 31].

The cost of distant recurrence, which included the acquisition and administration costs of therapies including CDK 4/6 inhibitors and mTOR inhibitors and follow-up and hospitalization expenditures, were estimated from the survey, based on subsequent lines of treatment for metastatic breast cancer (Supplementary Material) (Clinical Expert Survey, 2024). The costs of treating AML, CHF and the cost of terminal care were obtained from the literature and adjusted to 2024 using a medical-care specific inflation rate [32–35]. A summary of health-state costs is provided in the Supplementary Material.

The incidence of short-term AEs for anthracycline- and taxane-based regimens was based on a published Japanese study [36]. The incidence of short-term AEs associated with other regimens was based on a meta-analysis study, reporting an odds ratio applied to a reference paclitaxel-based regimen [37]. AEs were micro-costed by treatment setting (outpatient vs. inpatient), with the treatment received and health care resource use informed by the survey (Clinical Expert Survey, 2024).

Health state utilities for the Japanese specific population were sourced from the literature (Table 1). The utility values for recurrence-free health state (0.874) and distant recurrence (0.808) were sourced from reported values for primary breast cancer and metastatic breast cancer, respectively [38]. The AML utility value used (0.538) was sourced from the literature for relapsed AML, adjusted to account for chemotherapy [39, 40]. A value of 0.590 was used for CHF utility, sourced from a study that assessed the quality of life of Japanese patients implanted with a left ventricular assist device [41]. A one-off utility decrement was applied to all patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy to reflect the loss in utility associated with treatment administration and AEs [40]. All health state utilities were adjusted for background morbidity based on cohort age using age-specific general population utilities derived from Japanese EQ-5D norms sourced from the literature (Supplementary Materials) [42].
The model structure and model inputs were validated by an Advisory Board in 2024 (Advisory Board, 2024).

For the base case using the N0 population, the model reported total and disaggregated lifetime costs, life-years and QALYs for both the Oncotype DX test and clinico-pathological risk assessment, when used to guide treatment decisions in Japan. The primary outcome was the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER), defined as the incremental cost per incremental QALY gained. In Japan, the ICER is compared to the recommended willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of ¥5,000,000/QALY [43, 44]. Disaggregated costs included the cost of the Oncotype DX test, adjuvant endocrine and chemoendocrine therapy, short-term AEs, long-term AEs (AML and CHF), distant recurrence, and terminal care cost for breast cancer-related deaths. Life-years and QALYs accumulated by health state were presented for the Oncotype DX test and clinico-pathological risk assessment.

To understand the robustness of the model, uncertainty analyses conducted included deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA), probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) and scenario analyses. DSA is presented using a tornado plot (Supplementary Materials), representing the individual model inputs that had the most impact on the model results, where parameters were varied from the most plausible upper and lower value reported in the literature, or where not available, a 20% variation of the mean value was assumed [45]. PSA was performed by sampling the joint uncertainty of values for all model inputs simultaneously from pre-defined probability distributions using Monte Carlo simulation, with 5,000 model iterations. The PSA returned the average result for each of the model outcomes. The results of the PSA are presented using a scatter plot on a cost-effectiveness plane. Scenario analysis was conducted to test the underlying inputs and assumptions used in the analysis, with scenarios tested presented in Supplementary Material. Scenarios tested included alternative literature sources with real-world evidence for RS distribution, chemotherapy probabilities by RS results for the Oncotype DX test and clinical risk-based decisions, and assumptions related to distant recurrence probability, costs and health state utility.

A budget impact analysis (BIA) was conducted for a single year cohort population of N0 HR+/HER2- breast cancer who are eligible for chemotherapy and testing with the Oncotype DX test, using various cost-effectiveness time horizons (5-year, 10-year, and lifetime) to estimate patient costs. The model estimated patient numbers using the Japanese Ganjoho cancer statistics database, adjusted for the proportion in Japan with invasive breast cancer having the HR+/HER2- subtype and assumed 100% of patients were eligible for chemotherapy [3, 46]. The model estimated the difference in expenditures between (i) the original scenario, defined as using clinico-pathological risk assessment and no Oncotype DX test conducted, and (ii) the future scenario where 100% of patients were tested using the Oncotype DX test. Lifetime costs incurred per patient were tracked within the cost-effectiveness model. Local epidemiological data to estimate eligible patients were combined with the same clinical inputs as the cost-effectiveness analysis and used a Japanese public healthcare payer perspective (Table 1) [1, 3]. The impact of the proportion with the Oncotype DX test was also examined. Results are presented as undiscounted costs.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The Oncotype DX test was dominant (i.e., cost-saving and more effective) compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment in the overall node-negative (N0), HR+/HER2- early breast cancer patient population, generating more QALYs (0.207) at a lower cost (-¥649,596) for an average patient (Table 2). The largest reduction in costs was due to lower distant recurrence costs in the Oncotype DX group (-¥1,007,177) (Supplementary Material).

sec.p: The Oncotype DX test was also the dominant strategy across all subgroups, except for high clinical risk patients aged ≤ 50 years, for whom it was cost-effective (ICER = ¥66,807/QALY) at the Japanese willingness-to-pay threshold (Table 2).

Regarding the proportion of patients assigned to chemotherapy in the overall Oncotype DX group (Table 1), it was calculated as a weighted average of the proportion in each subgroup (≤ 50 years and > 50 years, low and high clinical risk) from the Clinical Expert Survey (Table S1). There was a general trend towards a higher proportion receiving chemotherapy in the ≤ 50 years subgroup and the subgroup of those at high clinical risk. Such treatment allocation was further guided by RS value, with an increasing chemotherapy proportion for higher RS value patients in the overall Oncotype DX group (Low RS: 0.2%, Intermediate RS: 0.6%~10.5%, High RS: 88.7%).

On the other hand, the proportion of patients assigned to chemotherapy in the overall comparator group of clinico-pathological risk assessment (Table 1) was also calculated as a weighted average of the proportion in each subgroup (≤ 50 years and > 50 years, low and high clinical risk) from the Clinical Expert Survey and complementary literature (Table S1). As in the Oncotype DX group, there was a general trend towards a higher proportion receiving chemotherapy in the ≤ 50 years subgroup and the subgroup of those at high clinical risk. However, there was no further differential treatment allocation based on RS value.

The total proportion of patients assigned to chemotherapy in the overall group was 23.8% when assessed using clinico-pathological risk assessment, compared to 15.7% when the Oncotype DX test was used (Fig. 3). Dividing patients further by different RS, the Oncotype DX test result was associated with a larger proportion of patients with a high RS receiving chemotherapy (12.4%) where the greatest benefit occurs, compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment (3.3%). For those high RS patients, treatment with chemotherapy resulted in less distant recurrence compared to treatment with endocrine therapy alone. The Oncotype DX test was also associated with a larger proportion of patients with low and intermediate RS receiving endocrine therapy alone (96.7%) compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment (79.5%). Those patients benefited from a reduction in chemotherapy-related long- and short-term AEs. In summary, the overall benefit was generated from (1) more patients with a high RS remaining recurrence-free with associated improved quality of life and extended life expectancy, and (2) fewer quality-of-life decrements for chemotherapy-related AEs in patients with a low or intermediate RS where the chemotherapy benefit is less.

sec.p: Based on the DSA, the largest driver of uncertainty in the model was the relative risk of distant recurrence with chemoendocrine therapy in patients with a high RS (Supplementary Material). Other inputs having an impact included chemotherapy allocation in patients with a high RS, discount rates for costs and clinical outcomes, and treatment duration for endocrine therapy in advanced disease. The use of the Oncotype DX test remained dominant for all parameters tested.

The PSA outcomes were similar to the deterministic results (Fig. 4), with mean incremental costs of -¥692,675 and incremental QALYs of 0.223. The Oncotype DX test was dominant in 96% of simulations, with a 99% probability of being cost-effective at the Japanese WTP threshold. The scenarios tested and rationale are provided in Supplementary Material). The Oncotype DX test remained dominant in all scenarios tested (Supplementary Material).

sec.p: The budget impact analysis was based on the annual expected number of N0 HR+/HER2- early breast cancer cases in Japan (45,760 cases per annum in 2022). Using lifetime costs for a single 1-year cohort, the Oncotype DX test was associated with cost savings of ¥43,398 million, when comparing the current scenario (using clinico-pathological risk assessment without the Oncotype DX test) (¥445,270 million) and future scenario (all eligible patients’ treatment was informed by the Oncotype DX test) (¥401,873 million). The largest cost saving was distant recurrence costs (¥60,306 million) (Supplementary Material). Improved budget impact was reported when the proportion tested with the Oncotype DX test was increased, with the Oncotype DX test generating cost savings when a 10 year cost-effectiveness time horizon is used for all proportions of the cohort tested (Fig. 5).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The use of the Oncotype DX test to inform treatment decisions was more effective and less costly compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment in the overall N0 HR+/HER2- early breast cancer population in Japan. Across all subgroups tested, the Oncotype DX test was cost saving or cost-effective using the recommended Japanese WTP threshold. The results align with previously published US and UK studies [16, 17].

Compared to decision-making based on clinico-pathological risk assessment, the Oncotype DX test guided treatment decisions in the adjuvant setting, where chemotherapy allocation was based on predicted clinical benefit reported from multiple randomized clinical trials. When evaluated with the Oncotype DX test, more patients in the high RS category received chemotherapy compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment. The clinical outcomes of using the Oncotype DX test were to reduce distant recurrence in patients with a high RS, and to minimize short-term AEs in patients with a low RS, for whom the clinical benefit from chemotherapy is minimal.

The Oncotype DX test was associated with a reduction in AML treatment costs and an increase in costs for CHF. Reduced treatment costs for AML were the result of an overall reduction in chemotherapy allocation for the Oncotype DX test compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment. Conversely, the incidence of CHF was higher with the use of the Oncotype DX test compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment, primarily due to the benefit of improved life expectancy.

Uncertainty analysis demonstrated the results were robust for all input parameters and the model assumptions used. The results remained dominant at both the most plausible lower and upper bounds for all model parameters. In addition, the PSA confirmed the robustness of the analysis where all parameters, when simultaneously varied, resulted in over 96% of model simulations predicting a dominant outcome and 99% predicting cost-effectiveness.

Extensive scenario analysis testing the assumptions used in the model confirmed the robustness of the analysis conclusions, which remained dominant in all scenarios tested. While the most robust evidence was used in the base case, alternative sources derived from the literature and clinical expert opinion were used to inform the following: (i) RS distribution, (ii) chemotherapy probability for patients tested with the Oncotype DX test and with clinico-pathological risk assessment, (iii) a 20% reduction in chemotherapy probability for a low RS and a 20% increase in chemotherapy probability for a high RS in the clinico-pathological risk assessment group, reflecting the impact of physician’s assessment in Japanese clinical practice. Other scenarios included alternative RS distributions for intermediate categories from TAILORx, distant recurrence probabilities being equal for chemoendocrine therapy and endocrine therapy, exclusion of AEs, costs and utility assumptions.

The BIA examined a typical annual incidence patient cohort expected to be diagnosed in Japan. The implementation of the Oncotype DX test results in an increased budget impact in Year 1. However, from Year 2 onwards, the annual net budget impact becomes negative, reflecting the cost-saving benefits associated with reduced disease recurrence. From Year 6, the total budget impact (sum of annual budget impact from Year 0) also turns negative due to the cost savings generated by the Oncotype DX test. This cost-saving effect for healthcare payers continues to grow throughout the entire analysis period (Year 0 to Year 37).

In order to ensure the analysis was applicable to the Japanese healthcare system, clinician survey results were used to inform Japanese-specific inputs (Clinical Expert Survey, 2024). The collected data were reviewed by two Japanese clinical experts and tested extensively using scenario analysis, an approach which was shown to be robust.

The results of this study were consistent with similar published studies reporting the cost-effectiveness of the Oncotype DX test. From a UK National Health Service and personal social services perspective, the use of the Oncotype DX test in N0, HR+/HER2- early breast cancer patients was dominant compared to clinico-pathological risk assessment when a lifetime horizon was considered. Similar to this study, the analysis was sensitive to the magnitude of the chemotherapy benefit in patients with a high RS [17]. A similar study comparing the Oncotype DX test with clinico-pathological risk assessment from a US societal perspective also showed the Oncotype DX test to be dominant, with an incremental 0.25 QALY benefit, and lower costs reported, using a lifetime horizon [16]. Both of these previously published studies applied country-specific inputs to reflect the local clinical treatment patterns.

Yamauchi et al. (2014) reported the comparison of the Oncotype DX test with clinico-pathological risk assessment in Japanese estrogen-receptor positive, N0 early breast cancer patients, with a reported ICER of ¥636,752/QALY [15] using a societal perspective. Our analysis reported the Oncotype DX test dominant versus clinico-pathological risk assessment. Several differences between studies were noted. Yamauchi’s study was published prior to TAILORx clinical trial and prior to the availability of CDK 4/6 inhibitors in advanced disease. At the time of publication of Yamauchi’s study, there was a lack of clear definition of clinical risk. In addition, chemotherapy allocation used in the Yamauchi study was overall higher compared to current clinical practice in Japan, resulting is a cost-effective outcome compared to dominance in our current analysis.

The analysis was limited by a number of factors. The analysis was based on the RS distribution and the distant recurrence probability from the TAILORx trial, which is the pivotal clinical evidence for the Oncotype DX test in N0 breast cancer. Distant recurrence rates were derived from the TAILORx trial for patients with a low or intermediate RS treated by endocrine therapy alone, and patients with an intermediate or high RS treated by chemoendocrine therapy. Distant recurrence rates for high RS patients treated with endocrine therapy alone were derived from the NSABP B-20 study [22], which were derived values based on the best available alternative evidence source [12]. Although the TAILORx trial and NSABP B-20 study did not include Japanese patients directly, no racial difference in the gene expression levels were noted in the evaluation dossier for PMDA, which supports the data suitability for application to a Japanese population.

A further limitation was uncertainty related to chemotherapy allocation when using the Oncotype DX test and clinico-pathological risk assessment, for each subgroup of patients with different clinical risk and age. Extensive testing of this limitation in scenario analysis did not alter the analysis conclusions; further real-world evidence in the Japanese setting would address this limitation.
Where possible, literature was used to inform model inputs; however, a Clinician Expert Survey was inform Japanese current clinical practice was assumed generalizable to Japanese clinical practice.

These results provide support for the use of the Oncotype DX test to guide treatment decisions in N0, HR+/HER2- early-stage breast cancer to improve patient outcomes in Japan. In addition, the use of the Oncotype DX test also resulted in net cost savings.

notes.title: Ethical approval
notes.p: This is a modelling study which did not require ethics approval.

notes.title: Informed consent
notes.p: Informed consent was not required as all data used was obtained from published clinical trials and publicly available sources, except when provided by clinical experts. The Clinician Expert Survey study was an opinion survey, based on the clinical experience of oncologists experienced in the treatment of early breast cancer in the adjuvant setting in Japan. Participating clinicians were aware it was an opinion survey study and agreed that the aggregated information would be used to provide up-to-date information related to current clinical practice for cost-effectiveness modelling. No individual patient data was used in the conduct of the study and therefore it was determined by the study coordinator that no ethics approval or formal waiver was required.
